analysis.one_liner: Offers Senate candidates full public campaign financing funded by spectrum fees instead of private donations.
analysis.headline: Introduced in March 2007 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, the Fair Elections Now Act never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a voluntary system in which Senate candidates who collect enough small $5 contributions from state residents could opt into public financing. They would then stop taking large private donations and receive public funds, broadcast vouchers, and discounted ad rates instead. The money would come from spectrum auction proceeds, a new fee on broadcasters' ad revenue, and a tax credit for voluntary donations. It also would have restricted congressional mass mailings before elections and tightened FEC reporting.
analysis.who_benefits: Senate candidates without personal wealth or connections to large donors could run competitive campaigns by qualifying through small-dollar support, and the bill's stated findings argue the change would make Senate elections more competitive [S3]. Voters would get guaranteed candidate debates [S3] and required disclosure from opposing candidates who spend heavily [S3]. The bill's own findings argue it would reduce the influence of large donors on legislation [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Candidates who gather 2,000 qualifying $5 contributions from state residents (plus 500 per extra congressional district) become 'participating candidates' eligible for Fund allocations of $750,000 plus $150,000 per additional district for the general election, with 67% of that for primaries, adjusted for media-market costs and inflation [S3].

Participating candidates must forgo large private contributions and personal-fund spending, may keep only limited 'seed money' of up to $100 per donor, and receive 'fair fight funds' matching money spent by or for their opponents, capped at 200% of their allocation [S3].
Participating general-election candidates receive broadcast advertisement vouchers worth $100,000 per congressional district and reduced TV ad rates (no more than 80% of the lowest unit charge) [S3].

The Fund would be financed by 10% of recovered spectrum auction proceeds, a 2% annual fee on broadcasters' gross advertising revenues, qualifying contributions, penalties, and voluntary donations eligible for a tax credit of up to $500 [S3].

The bill requires participating candidates to take part in at least one primary and two general-election public debates, and restricts franked mass mailings by members during the 90 days before primary and general elections [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Broadcasters would pay a new 2% fee on gross advertising revenues, sell ad time to participating candidates at up to 20% off, and must accept vouchers as payment [S3]. Large political donors and interests that finance campaigns would lose their channel of influence over participating candidates [S3]. Federal revenue would be reduced by the 10% spectrum auction diversion and the new donation tax credit [S3].

drawbacks.text: The program depends on money that otherwise goes to the Treasury: 10% of recovered spectrum auction proceeds is diverted to the Fund and voluntary donations earn a tax credit of up to $500, so taxpayers bear the program's cost through foregone revenue [S3].

Participation is voluntary, so a candidate who declines could still raise and spend unlimited private money; while fair fight funds respond to opposing spending, they are capped at 200% of the allocation, which a critic could argue leaves participating candidates underfunded in very expensive races [S3].

Fair fight funds are triggered by opponent and outside spending, meaning every dollar spent against a participating candidate draws more public money into the race, which could increase total campaign spending rather than reduce it [S3].

Broadcasters bear direct costs: a 2% fee on gross advertising revenue and mandatory discounted rates plus voucher acceptance, and the bill includes a 'review of constitutional issues' section, reflecting that mandatory broadcast terms and campaign-finance rules faced likely legal challenge [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered a genuine structural change: it would have let candidates run statewide Senate campaigns on small-dollar support and public funds, weakening the role of large donors. The costs are real but modest — foregone federal revenue and new obligations on broadcasters — and the voluntary design means privately funded candidates could still outspend participants. The design questions (voluntary participation, fair-fight escalation, constitutionality) were ones the bill itself built a review commission to revisit [S3].

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and sat there without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote until the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Sen. Durbin introduced S. 936, the Fair Elections Now Act, in the Senate on March 20, 2007, with Sen. Specter joining as the bill's other introducer [S1].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day; that referral is the last action recorded in its history for the 110th Congress [S5].
The bill attracted 3 cosponsors (1 Republican, 2 Democrats) during the Congress, but the Finance Committee never reported the bill and the full Senate never voted on it [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent senators and the large private donors who finance Senate campaigns kept the existing system, and broadcasters avoided the new spectrum fee and discounted ad rates. No voter-facing change occurred.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large donors, incumbent senators, and broadcasters

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — a Democratic sponsor with a Republican co-introducer and 3 cosponsors split 2 D / 1 R [S3][S4] — but no vote was ever taken, so no party breakdown of support on the merits exists.

industries.note: The bill would impose a 2% annual fee on broadcasters' gross advertising revenues, cap what participating candidates can be charged at 80% of the lowest ad rate, require stations to accept vouchers as payment, and bar preempting candidate ads [S3]. Broadcast advertising is a major revenue source during election years, so broadcasters had a direct financial stake in the bill's failure.

industries.industry: Large political donors and moneyed interests
industries.note: The bill would have cut off the large private contributions that finance Senate campaigns, offering candidates a public-funding alternative instead [S3]. Donors who give to gain access to lawmakers would lose that channel for participating candidates.

Public allocations, vouchers, and fair fight funds would route campaign media spending through participating candidates, sustaining ad spending, but the broadcast rate discounts and audits would compress margins [S3].

The bill would cut the coordinated-expenditure limit for parties backing participating candidates but lets candidates transfer voucher value to party committees, giving parties a new funding channel with conditions attached [S3].
